The climate crisis is no longer a distant threat. It is here, shaping our present and defining our future. Rising seas, extreme heat, floods, wildfires, and devastating storms disrupt lives across the globe. Families are being displaced. Farmers are losing crops. Children are growing up in a world of uncertainty. Those least responsible are often the hardest hit. But this is not just a story of crisis. It's a story of possibility. Because we are on the cusp of the clean energy era, the renewables revolution. Leaders, now is the time to seize the biggest economic opportunity of our lifetime. With national climate plans, we have the blueprints for successful economies and societies, creating jobs, expanding investments, and building opportunities for all, saving lives and safeguarding public health, building energy independence and security, connecting communities and upholding Indigenous rights. limiting increasingly dangerous and costly impacts of climate change, protecting nature and biodiversity, which protects us all. This is our moment of opportunity. Let's seize it.

Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, friends, colleagues, good afternoon. For those of you who don't know me, my name is Melissa Fleming. I am the UN Under-Secretary-General for Global Communications, and it is my honor to moderate the special event on climate convened by His Excellency, Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, and His Excellency, Mr. Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, President of Brazil, who will be with us any time now. The Secretary General and President Lula have agreed to work together to mobilize increased action on climate ahead of COP 30, which Brazil will host in November. Against the backdrop of a worsening climate crisis and challenging geopolitics, we are here today to discuss the steps we can collectively take to accelerate the just energy transition, to strengthen climate justice for developing countries, and to protect our natural world. We have all the solutions we need to limit temperature rise to 1.5 degrees. What we need today is action. Excellencies, we will start with a scientific assessment of the current efforts to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement, and this will be presented by Professor Johan Johan Rockstrom, Director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, and Professor Katharine Hayhoe from Texas Tech University. Professors, you have the floor.

Thank you. Good afternoon, your excellencies, co-citizens on planet Earth. It's now 10 years since the world in Paris entered the legally binding agreement to avoid dangerous climate change. Since then, science has become overwhelmingly clear. Allowing long-term global warming to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius constitutes danger. And yet, greenhouse gas emissions continue rising, and in 2024, annual global temperature change was pushed beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius for the first time on our watch. This is a deep concern. An even deeper concern is that warming appears to be accelerating, outpacing emissions. The long-term average warming is now between 1.3 and 1.4 degrees. We are on a path to breach 1.5 degrees Celsius multi-decadal boundary within the next 5, 10 years, a temperature we've not experienced over the past 100,000 years. Here we must admit failure. failure to protect peoples and nations from unmanageable impacts of human-induced climate change. But we don't have to keep failing. Returning to below 1.5 degrees by the end of this century must remain the obligation for all international efforts to limit dangerous climate change. Extreme heats, fire, droughts, water scarcity, flooding, and land degradation, reinforced by us, are already impacting the lives of billions of people around the world. Beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius, these dangers will become increasingly unmanageable. Every tenth of a degree of avoided warming matters, saves lives and livelihoods. This is not a time for resignation. Beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius, there's also a real risk of crossing tipping points. The most recent science concludes that we're therefore dangerously close to triggering fundamental and irreversible change. If we make the right choices going forward, though, there is still an overshoot pathway that can bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees Celsius by the end of this century. Such a narrow escape remains possible, but it will be extremely challenging. It requires deep and rapid reduction of all greenhouse gases, involving a near-complete transition, starting now, away from fossil fuels. We also know that cutting emissions won't be enough. we need to massively scale up carbon dioxide removal. For every 0.1 degree Celsius of planetary cooling, 200 billion tons are needed to be removed from the atmosphere. But even if this succeeds, we fail unless we safeguard the world's most powerful carbon sink and planetary cooling system, a healthy planet. If we don't return to the safe operating space of the nine planetary boundaries that regulates Earth's stability, including biodiversity, pollutants, land, nutrients, and the ocean, a safe climate future is out of reach, irrespective of our mitigation efforts. Don't be fooled. We are currently following a path that will take us to three degrees Celsius in just 75 years, shorter than the existence of this very institution, an existential threat we have not experienced in the last 3 million years. And there's no guarantee that efforts to cool the planet will succeed. So my message today, science is clear. We have a planetary crisis on our watch, and we do have scalable solutions for phasing out fossil fuels, efficient resource use, and transformation to healthy and sustainable food, pathways that makes us all winners. The window to a manageable climate future is still open, but just. Failure is not inevitable. It is a choice. Thank you. And with that, I pass on to my-- And with that, I pass on to my dear colleague, Professor Katherine Hayhoe.

Thank you. As Dr. Rockstrom indicated, we are conducting an unprecedented and perilous experiment with Earth, our only home. The science is clear. Right now, according to natural factors, the planet should be getting slowly cooler. Instead, it is warming faster and faster. And we are responsible for all of that warming. The science is also clear that every additional bit of warming matters. For every 10th of a degree, we can put a number on how much worse it gets. Billions of dollars in flood, wildfire, and storm damage, millions of avoidable deaths from extreme heat, air pollution, and more. Now, steady increases in heat waves and crop losses are bad enough, but the further we go past 1 and 1/2 degrees C, the greater the risk of the dangerous tipping points Dr. Rockstrom warned us about. So the obvious question is, if the science is this clear, and it is, and it has been for decades, then why haven't we fixed this already? Despite decades of deliberate disinformation that continues to be amplified today, the majority of people know the four basics. Most people know climate change is real, it is human caused, It is serious, and the experts agree. These four things make us worried. And yet, even though the majority of people in almost every country around the world, including this one, are already worried about climate change, awareness does not necessarily lead to action. Too often, we think if we just explain the facts more clearly, that will be enough, but it isn't. Because if we don't know what to do, we'll do nothing. To act, we need to know two more things. We need to know that we are not alone. Others care, and we need to know that there is hope. Hope is not wishful thinking. Hope is knowing that if we act, it will make a difference. And that is exactly what the science says, every action matters. When it comes to climate solutions, there's no one action that will fix it all, but there are so many that together give us more than enough to meet our climate goals. Transitioning from the dirty fossil fuels of the past to the clean energy of the future, protecting and restoring ecosystems that absorb carbon and shelter us from flood and heat, transforming food systems to reduce waste and emissions, Investing in resilience so the most vulnerable communities benefit most. We cannot prevent this catastrophe alone, but together we can by setting stronger targets, by moving faster timelines, and by making deeper commitments. Why? Because the science tells us that every bit of warming matters, every year matters, every choice matters, not to the planet, the planet will endure, it matters to us. When I had a child, I made the biggest wager anyone can place on the future. And you may have done that too. The scariest part is that the outcome of that bet doesn't depend on me alone. It depends on all of us, on our willingness to choose courage over fear, action over delay, and most of all, hope over despair. I believe it's a bet we can still win, and that's why every day I practice hope, not as a feeling, but as a discipline, one that's essential to the fight ahead. I won't give up on a better future, and I hope you won't either, because what's at stake is nothing less than everything and everyone we love.
Thank you, Professor Rockstrom and Professor He Ho, and every day we will all practice hope as well. It's now my honor to invite the Secretary General to the podium to deliver his remarks.

Excellencies, dear friends, as we have just heard, it is still possible to limit global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees by century's end. We know what permanently breaching that limit would mean for people and planet. The science compels climate action, so does the economics. Clean energy is powering jobs, growth and sustainable development, generating the fastest and cheapest electricity, insulating economies from volatile fossil fuel markets, providing energy security and sovereignty, and helping to deliver clean and affordable energy for all. Despite vast fossil fuel subsidies, distorting markets, clean energy received double the investment of fossil fuels last year. The bottom line, clean is competitive and climate action is imperative. Excellencies, the Paris Agreement has made a difference. In the last 10 years, projected global temperature rise has dropped from 4 degrees Celsius to less than 3 if current NDCs are fully implemented. Now, we need new plans for 2035 that go much further and much faster. delivering dramatic emissions cuts aligned with 1.5 degrees, covering all emissions and sectors, and accelerating a just energy transition globally. Your new plans can take us a significant step forward. A UN report will calculate their impact for global emissions. If they fall short, We must create the conditions for a decade of acceleration. We know it can be done. China met its 2030 wind and solar target six years ahead of schedule. India reached 50% electricity capacity from non-fossil fuels five years early. We are in the dawn of a new energy era. We must seize this moment of opportunity. COP30 in Brazil must conclude with a credible global response plan to get us on track. Five areas are crucial. First, energy. Fossil fuels still dominate. We must supercharge the clean energy transition, investing in grids and storage to unlock the full potential of renewables. lowering capital costs for developing countries, and redirecting fossil fuel subsidies to adjust the transition. Second, methane, a potent global heating gas. Drastic cuts this decade are essential, and most can be achieved quickly and cheaply. The International Energy Agency estimates fossil fuel operations could cut 40% of methane emissions today with no net costs. Third, forests. We must end the destruction of nature's greatest carbon sinks. This could deliver a fifth of needed emissions reductions by 2030. Fourth, heavy industry. We have seen important advances in technologies to cut emissions from steel and cement and heavy transport. They must be deployed urgently. Fifth, climate justice. Developing countries that did least to cause the crisis are suffering the most. Climate disasters are inflicting damages that exceed the GDP of some small islands. Droughts and floods are taking lives, fueling anger and inflaming conflict. all while finance gaps prevent investments in adaptation and resilience. We need urgent action to unlock funds for developing countries to seize clean energy benefits and protect lives and economies. And that requires reforming the international financial architecture to strengthen developing countries' participation. We need effective debt relief and scaled up solutions like debt swaps and disaster pause clauses. We need a major increase in the lending capacity of multilateral development banks and significant contributions to the loss and damage fund, including from innovative sources, and a major boost in adaptation finance with developing countries meeting their pledge to double funding this year. COP30. must show a credible path to mobilizing the 1.3 trillion US dollars annually in climate finance by 2035 as agreed at COP29 in Baku. Identifying sources, existing and new, outlining policies, instruments and actions to make finance accessible, affordable and at scale, and establishing credible accountability measures to verify progress. Excellencies, the science demands action. The law commands it. The economics compel it. And people are calling for it. I look forward to hearing how you will respond, and the UN stands ready to help you to deliver. Thank you very much.
Thank you, Secretary-General. I now have the honor to invite His Excellency Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, President of Brazil, to deliver his remarks.

Well, I'd like to... greet our Secretary General and say to him how happy I am to be taking part at this high level event on climate action. Less than 50 days stand between this meeting and COP30. It is time to ask whether the world will arrive in Berlin with its homework done. The Paris Agreement gave countries the freedom to set emission reduction targets consistent with their realities and capacities. But the submission of nationally determined contributions is not an option. As it was made clear by the International Court of Justice, it is an obligation. In a world where serious violations have become commonplace, failing to submit an NDC may seem like a lesser evil. But without the collection of NDCs, the planet is moving in the dark. Only with a full picture will we know where we are going and at what pace. Today, the countries gathered here are fulfilling their duty, but there are others that have not yet done so. The denialism we face is not only related to climate, it is multilateral. No one is safe from the effects of climate change. Walls at borders will not stop droughts or storms. Nature does not bow down to bombs or warships. No country stands above another. The risk of unilateralism is the chain reaction it provokes. Each broken commitment is an invitation to new isolated actions. The result is a vicious cycle of mistrust and paralysis. We need to restore confidence and conviction in collective mobilization. If it were not for the Paris Agreement, we would already be on track for a 4 degree rise in Earth's average temperature. And if we are able to protect the ozone layer, we can also stop global warming. Fatalism is the worst enemy of action. The energy transition opens the door to a productive and technological transformation comparable to the Industrial Revolution. Nationally determined contributions are the roadmap that will guide each country through this change. They are not mere numbers or percentages. They are an opportunity to rethink models and reorient policies and investments toward a new economic paradigm. For this to happen on a global scale, wealthy nations need to bring forward their climate neutrality targets and expand access to resources and technologies for developing countries. The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities remains valid. Brazil was the second country to present its new NDC. We are committed to reducing emissions of all greenhouse gases by between 59 and 67 percent, covering all sectors of the economy. Our goal of ending deforestation by 2030 will continue to help make this objective a reality. By hosting COP in the Amazon, Brazil wants to show that it is impossible to preserve nature without caring for people. There is no way to revolutionize our relationship with the planet without engaging a wide range of stakeholders. This is why we promoted the global ethical stocktake with six regional dialogues that included representatives from civil society, the private sector, indigenous peoples and traditional communities, scientists, artists, religious leaders and local authorities. The voice of the people must reach heads of state and government. We want to promote a leaders' summit that fosters a frank and direct dialogue worthy of the mission entrusted to us by our societies. We have the chance to right injustices and build a prosperous and sustainable future for everyone. Thus, I call on the countries that have not yet submitted their NDCs. The success of COP30 in Belen depends on you. Let us make the Amazon the stage for a decisive moment in the history of multilateralism. I have said and have been saying that COP30, Mr. Secretary General, is the COP of truth. This COP is going to have to say whether or not we believe what science is showing us, if we leaders, heads of states, if we trust or don't trust science, because we're going to have to make a decision, because if we do not make a decision, society is going to stop believing its leaders. And instead of strengthening the struggle against global warming, we are going to help discredit multilateralism, policies, and democracy. And all of us will lose because denialism may actually win. Thus, the ball is in COP30's court, and I hope to rely on all of you and see all of you there. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President. And now let me open the floor to heads of state and government and excellencies. In the interest of time and ensuring that all participants get to speak, I encourage you to keep your interventions to maximum a maximum of three minutes. Leaders will speak from one of the lecterns at the front of the room. You'll be escorted from your seats to the lectern by UN protocol. To begin, I am delighted to introduce His Excellency Xi Jinping, President of the People's Republic of China.

Your Excellency, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Your Excellency, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, colleagues, this year marks the 10th anniversary of the Paris Agreement, a pivotal year for countries to submit their new nationally determined contributions. Global climate governance is entering a key stage. I wish to share with you three points. First, we must firm up confidence. Green and low-carbon transition is the trend of our time. While some country is acting against it, the international community should stay focused on the right direction, remain unwavering in confidence, unremitting in actions, and unrelenting in intensity. and push for formulation and delivery on NDCs, with a view to providing more positive energy to the cooperation on global climate governance. Second, we must live up to responsibilities. In the course of global green transition, fairness and equity should be upheld, and the right to development of developing countries fully respected. The transition should serve to narrow rather than widen the North-South gap. Countries need to honor principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, whereby developed countries should take the lead in fulfilling emission reduction obligations and provide more financial and technological support to developing countries. Third, we must deepen cooperation. The world now faces a huge demand for green development. It is important that countries strengthen international coordination in green technologies and industries to address the shortfall in green production capacity and ensure free flow of quality green products globally so that the benefits of green development can reach all corners of the world. Colleagues, let me take this opportunity to announce China's new NDCs as follows. China will, by 2035, reduce economy-wide net greenhouse gas emissions by 7% to 10% from peak levels, striving to do better, increase the share of non-fossil fuels in total energy consumption to over 30 percent. Expand the installed capacity of wind and solar power to over six times the 2020 levels, striving to bring the total to 3,600 gigawatts. Scale up the total forest stock volume to over 24 billion cubic meters. Make new energy vehicles the mainstream in the sales of new vehicles. Expand the national carbon emissions trading market to cover major high emission sectors, and basically establish a climate-adaptive society. These targets represent China's best efforts based on the requirements of the Paris Agreement. Meeting these targets requires both painstaking efforts by China itself and a supportive and open international environment. We have the resolve and confidence to deliver on our commitments. Colleagues, great visions require concrete actions. Climate response is an urgent yet long-term task. Let's all step up our actions to realize the beautiful vision of harmony between man and nature and preserve planet Earth, the place we call home. Thank you.
I thank the President of China for his statement and now welcome Her Excellency Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, to come to the podium.

President Lula, Secretary-General Guterres, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Indeed, 10 years have passed since we adopted the Paris Agreement, and since then, the world has changed. Let me give you just three figures. Since Paris, renewable energy has increased by 140%. Investment in clean energy has increased by almost 80%. And carbon pricing in countries has doubled from 40 to 80. So the clean transition is moving on. And let me assure you, Europe will stay the course on our climate ambition. Our emissions are down nearly 40% since 1990. They now represent only 6% of global emissions. We are on track to reach our 2030 target, that is to cut emissions by minus 55%. And I'm happy to announce that last week, member states agreed that our national determined contribution would range between 66% and 72%. So work is advancing, and we will formally submit our NDC ahead of COP30. But in parallel, we are also looking ahead. We're working on a 2040 target of a proposed 90% emission reduction. That is our way to climate neutrality by 2050. And my message is that the world can count on European Union's continued climate leadership. My second point, we're doubling down on global partnerships. Because the question is no longer if the transition will occur and how fast, but who will benefit? Europe's answer is clear. All countries worldwide should reap the benefits, especially the most vulnerable. And that is why we will remain the world's largest providers of climate finance. In addition, we will mobilize up to 300 billion euros to support the clean transition worldwide through our Global Gateway investment program. And we will turn our collective agreement to triple renewable energy by 2030 into a reality. We support, for example, over 300 million people in Africa to give them access to electricity and clean cooking. And this is not only a climate issue. This is about basic human dignity, because no mother, no child should die because simply cooking dinner under abhorrent circumstances. Ladies and gentlemen, President Lula will soon welcome us to the Amazon, the green lungs of our planet. There could be no better place to reaffirm our strong commitment to multilateralism. So let's get it done. Thank you very much.
I thank the President of the European Commission and welcome now His Excellency, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, President of the Republic of Turkey.

Distinguished heads of state and government, Mr. Secretary-General, I greet you all with most heartfelt feelings. I wish Brazil success as it prepares to host the 30th climate conference in November. The climate law, which we adopted last July, was a significant step for us towards reaching our 2053 net zero emissions target. Our endeavors to establish an emissions trading system, implement a green finance strategy, and to create a national green taxonomy are all ongoing. We have built our climate policy on seven pillars: energy, industry, buildings, transportation, waste, agriculture, and forestry. We have also formulated our second nationally determined contribution to cover all sectors and all greenhouse gases. Through the policies to be implemented in the economy, we aim to achieve an emission reduction of 466 million tons by 2035, and to lower our emissions down to 643 million tons. While increasing the share of renewable energy and improving energy efficiency, we are expanding low carbon technologies in industry. As of this year, we have raised the share of renewable energy within the total installed capacity up to more than 60%. 2053, I'm sorry, we are rapidly reinforcing our infrastructure, particularly electric vehicle production, and we are prioritizing railway investments. In line with our 2053 net zero emissions target, we will continue to transform our key sectors. Now, access to international financing and cooperation in the field of technology, both of these are essential to be able to achieve these goals. I would like to underline particularly that our water efficiency campaign and the zero waste initiative led under the auspices of my spouse, Emine Erdogan, and elevated to the global level, both of these play a critical role in our fight against climate change. And we hope to crown all these efforts by hosting the 31st COP, Conference of the Parties. in 2026. So, with these thoughts in mind, I wish this climate summit to yield beneficial results, and I once again extend my greetings to you all with kind regards.
I thank the President of the Republic of Turkey. And now ask His Excellency, Anthony Albanese, Prime Minister of the Commonwealth of Australia, come to the podium.

Well, thank you very much, Secretary General, colleagues. This is the decisive decade for acting on the environmental challenge of climate change, but also seizing the economic opportunities of clean energy. We all grasp the scale and the urgency of our task. We all understand the consequences of inaction for our environment, for our economies, for our people's way of life, and for our children's future. Australians know the toll taken by extreme weather events becoming more frequent and more intense, the devastation that cyclones, floods, bushfires, and drought inflict on our communities. And Australia knows that we are not alone. We are all involved. An essential message that each of us can send to our citizens is this: it is not too late. If we act now and move with common purpose, then we can do more than just guard against the very worst. We can protect our environment and build a stronger and fairer economy for the next generation. That is the optimism and determination that Australia brings to this task. And today I present Australia's next nationally determined contribution. Australia's 2035 target is to reduce emissions by 62 to 70% on 2005 levels. This target is ambitious, but importantly, it is also achievable. It is backed by the independent scientific advice of our climate change authority. It will mean that over the next decade we halve our current level of emissions. And it will ensure that Australia honours our commitment to the Paris Agreement and its goal of keeping global temperatures below dangerous levels. Setting targets and showing ambition matters. It provides accountability for government and certainty for private sector investment. What is most important is having the practical plan to reach our goal. And that is where Australian clean energy is the key. Just as our traditional resources have helped to power the extraordinary economic transformation of our region, our renewables can underpin new prosperity for the growing economies of the Indo-Pacific. And our Pacific family is partnering with Australia in our bid to host COP31 in next year. We want to bring the world with us on climate change, not by asking any nation to forgo the jobs or security that its people deserve, but by working with every nation to seize and share those opportunities. None of us can succeed alone, but together we cannot fail. I thank you.
I thank the Prime Minister of Australia and now ask His Excellency, Serenjal S. Whipps, Jr., President of the Republic of Palau, to come to the floor.

President Lula, Secretary-General, Excellencies, colleagues, distinguished guests, it is my distinct honor to speak to you on behalf of the 39 members of the Alliance of Small Island States, whose people are the most vulnerable, living daily with the stark reality of climate change. Rising seas, stronger storms, and changing ecosystems are not projections for us. They are our lived experience, and they threaten our very survival. This summit is a key milestone on the road to COP30, a COP at which the outcome must be nothing less than transformational. It must deliver new commitments that keep us firmly on the pathway to limit warming to 1.5. The science is unequivocal. This is a critical decade. Delay is defeat. Every fraction of a degree beyond 1.5 brings irreversible loss, especially for the vulnerable people of small islands. We come here with firm expectations that new climate commitments in the form of 1.5 aligned nationally determined contributions would be submitted in time to be included in the synthesis report ahead of COP30. And I must speak plainly to major emitters. Your leadership will define the outcome. Those with the greatest responsibility and the greatest capacity to act must do far more. Align your economies with 1.5, phase out fossil fuels, and accelerate the transition to clean energy and ensure that your actions inspire confidence, not doubt, in the multilateral process. The recent opinion from the ICJ has reaffirmed that what IOS has long said, climate action is not optional. It is an obligation grounded in international law and in the principles of equity and justice. The world must look to this opinion as a moral and legal compass, underscoring that failure to act is failure to meet international duty. Excellencies, the measure of leadership at this summit and at COP30 is whether we choose short-term convenience for some or long-term survival for all peoples. For small island developing states, there is no margin for delay. We urge all countries, especially those major emitters, to deliver an outcome at COP30 that is ambitious, just, and firmly aligned with 1.5, this decade and not the next. We urge you to lead by example as we face these interconnected challenges together. Let us turn these challenges into opportunities, and we know it is technically and financially possible, but time is running short to act. Small island developing states are leading the way in climate ambition, and I am proud to highlight the leadership of my country. Palau today holds a rare net negative status. Our forests absorb more than six times the greenhouse gases we emit. But we are not stopping there. By 2035, we are committing to slash emissions by 44% compared to 2015 levels. We've broadened our targets across more sectors, such as oceans, but we cannot do it on our own. We need stronger support for implementation, and we are also not alone. Other SIDS are stepping up with bold commitments too, and Palau is committed to submitting our NDC 3.0 ahead of COP30. For SIDS, ambition alone is not enough. Implementation demands resources and fairness. And we call for scaled up, predictable climate finance to support both mitigation, adaptation, and loss and damage. The pledges of the past must now be met with delivery. This includes new and additional finance, not repackaged promises. Further adaptation to climate impacts is fundamentally important to SIDS, and we are looking to We'll be looking to COP30 to finally deliver an operational global goal on adaptation that includes the resources necessary to turn plans into action. The world is watching. Our people are waiting. And our survival depends on what we decide together now. The future we shape must be one which guarantees dignity, justice, and opportunity for all. I thank you.
I thank the Chair of AOSIS and President of the Republic of Palau. And our next speaker is His Excellency Muhammad Shafiqul Islam Sharif, Prime Minister of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan.

President Luna de Silva, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, As-salamu alaykum and a very good afternoon. As I speak to you, my country is reeling from intense monsoon rains, cloudburst, flash floods, mudslides, and devastating urban flooding. This climate-induced catastrophe has impacted over 5 million lives across 4,100 villages. Over 1,000 precious lives have been lost. We are facing this calamity at a time when the scars of the 2022 floods that inflicted losses exceeding $30 billion and displaced millions are still visible across our land. And Secretary Guterres is a witness to this catastrophe. Ladies and gentlemen, Pakistan's contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions is almost negligible, but we bear impacts far beyond our share. Our commitment to delivering on our Climate agenda, however, remains steadfast and unwavering. In our 2021 nationally determined contribution, Pakistan committed to an unconditional 15% reduction in projected greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 as part of an overall target of cutting emissions by 50% I'm pleased to share that Pakistan has already delivered on its unconditional pledge of a 15% reduction. Renewables are presently providing over 32% of Pakistan's power mix. Solar energy has grown sevenfold since 2021. 23,000 hectares of mangroves have been restored. However, the implementation of Pakistan's national adaptation plan is hampered and hampered severely due to inadequate international climate finance. Ladies and gentlemen, I am pleased to announce here that we shall increase the share of renewables and hydropower to 62% of our energy mix by 2035, expanding nuclear energy capacity by 1,200 megawatt by 2030, shifting 30% of transport to cleaner mobility by 2030, and establishing 3,000 charging stations nationwide, scaling up climate-smart agriculture, safeguarding water security, and advancing the plantation of 1 billion trees. Excellencies, in conclusion, may I say, while Pakistan is willing and determined to be part of the solution to the climate crisis, we hope and expect that the international community will also honor its commitment for the sake of our future generations. And my last line is that loans over loans, adding to loans, is not the solution. Thank you very much, and God bless you.

I thank the Prime Minister of Pakistan, and the Secretary-General has to leave now, and I believe also for a meeting with the Security Council. I believe, President Lula, you also need to depart, or you could stay for a little while. Okay. Our next speaker is Her Excellency Maya Amor-Motley, Prime Minister of Barbados.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair, President Lula, Madam Deputy Secretary-General, my sister, distinguished guests, distinguished colleagues all. We gather here today not simply to speak about climate ambition, but to demand climate action of ourselves and of each other. Barbados' NDC sits within a framework of our investment plan for prosperity and resilience. We've estimated that this plan will cost us about $11.6 billion between now and the next decade. And that of that, $5 billion is likely to be public sector driven. We recognize that if this is to be real, we have to take the world as we find it, and we have to understand how we're going to finance it, and we have to understand how we are going to have access to the goods that are necessary, even if we find the finance, because very often small states cannot have control over the supply chain and fall down in its ability to execute. At the same time, when we ask of others, we do not absent ourselves from the obligation of performance. And what do I mean by that? The Bridgetown Initiative speaks not just of asking for concessional funding from the world, but also of greater domestic resource mobilization. We have determined that every citizen must share the burden in order to share the bounty of a clean and proper and fit environment. We ask our citizens as employees to be able and as self-employed to contribute point two five percent of all their wages and earnings and we as government go the extra mile and we will contribute 0.35% of GDP every year into a resilience and regeneration fund. We continue to try to innovate because in the world where we are not winning the battle of longer capital and cheaper capital, we need therefore to innovate. And whether it is debt swaps or whether it is natural disaster clauses, which the market has just shown it will accept, when we issued a US$500 million bond two months ago, we need to be able to use all of these instruments to ensure that the NDCs do not just become an archival document but a lived reality for our people. At the same time, we need to recognize that if we are going to reduce emissions, And I say this to you, President Lula, as we go into COP, we had a voluntary agreement on methane out of Dubai. That is not enough. We need a legally binding global agreement for methane reduction. The fossil fuel industry is not the enemy. It is the emissions. And if we have a legally binding methane agreement, we can buy ourselves time over the next 15 or 20 years to give them sufficient time to continue to do superfast research to scale up decarbonising technology to commercial level, while at the same time giving countries in the south the opportunity not to have to abandon the one thing that can finance their way to net zero. That makes sense for the oil and gas people and for the planet. It makes sense for the farmers and for the planet. Quite frankly, we cannot continue as if things are still the same. If we want the NDCs to be appropriately applied, we have to find a way to buy time. That allows everybody to stay in the game, and it allows those who believe and those who do not believe to work in common purpose. I look forward to our being able not just to execute our NDCs in terms of ambition, but also for us to have an additional discussion urgently. I feel that we do not need to reinvent the wheel. The Montreal Protocol that allowed us to reduce HFCs is the most successful

climate agreement in history. We can replicate it with no more than a two or three page agreement on the reduction of methane as a matter of legally binding obligations. Thank you.
I thank the Prime Minister of Barbados for her statement and invite as our next speaker, His Excellency Gabriel Boric, President of the Republic of Chile.

Thank you very much. Good afternoon to all those present here. All protocols observed. With respect to this meeting, all of the countries who are part of this institution must make our NDCs at the national level, the NDCs, and we must tackle with determination the challenges of global climate financing. And this takes place in a turbulent world where, unfortunately, we hear strong voices that minimize or even deny the reality of climate change, of the climate crisis. And in the light of these voices, we have to respond with firmness. There's no more time to lose. Surely the rich countries are not going to pay for the consequences. or like poor countries or developing countries with respect to the consequences of climate change. This denialism is particularly dangerous. We can discuss without any doubt, in a legitimate discussion, how can we tackle, what are the best strategies, what do we have to do to tackle the climate crisis, what countries have more or less responsibilities, what are the timelines involved, but we cannot discuss or we cannot question that there is a climate crisis. And this is a lie if we do that, and lying is not good. We shouldn't relativize this, it's not an opinion, we have to Face the lies. And those who with power affirm that there is no climate crisis, they are passing those costs on to the poor countries. And in the light of this, all of the members of the United Nations, we should stand up and reveal ourselves. The transition that we need, we know cannot wait. It has to be sped up, but it also be fair as well. The richer countries have to take the first step and have to assume the responsibility that falls upon them as being the main emitter of carbon throughout history, being committed to the world to reduce their emissions more rapidly and support the transition in developing countries, the same ones that today are the most vulnerable in the light of climate change. And let me tell you something with a great deal of affection, because we have a great deal of respect and a very rich relationship with the members of the European Union. Accepting, as most countries have done, accepting the increase and raising defense expenditure to 5%, that is unacceptable. They are forcing them to raise their defense expenditure. And the defense expenditure is one of the most polluting factors. And of course, we welcome the fact when they say we're going to reduce our emissions by 70%. But at the same time, on the other hand, they are increasing their investments in war. And investing in war is not a very good investment. must invest more in peace and in how we can improve conditions for developing countries for this would be a fair and a just climate change. In Latin America and the Caribbean, we know what is at stake, and that is why we support decisively President Lula and the organization of the summit. In Colombia, we are updating our NDCs. In Chile, rather, we are increasing our NDCs. We have set the timeline by 2035 as a step towards carbon neutrality, and this will happen in 2070, and I hope we'll do it before. Chile, furthermore, has had a strategy which has pointed to different sectors of the economy, from mining to transportation. Santiago de Chile, our capital, is the capital of the world outside of China that has more electric. And we are looking at these. We have areas that were polluted for a long time, and now we are improving that. Thanks to all those who are committed to this. Today, we are the ones, the decision makers, who can change the course of the world, not for us, but for the upcoming generations. And we have a responsibility, and history will judge us for this. Thank you.
I thank the President of the Republic of Chile and now welcome as our next speaker, His Excellency Taye Ake Selassie Amde, President of the Federal Republic of Ethiopia.

Excellencies, heads of state and governments, ladies and gentlemen, I would like to thank His Excellency President Lula da Silva and Madam Deputy Secretary General for convening this meeting. As we look forward for a much anticipated COP30 in Belem, Brazil, Ethiopia together with other African Union and African countries had the honor of hosting the second climate summit early this month. The summit involving nearly 25,000 participants from all over the stakeholders was a successful event that sets out Africa climate priorities. The outcome declaration encompass a commitment that Africa is not merely a victim of climate change, but a proactive force in developing innovative and sustainable solution. I thank the organizers for this opportunity to share the main outcomes of the African Climate Summit as reflected in the Addis Ababa Declaration. It is our hope and expectation that these main deliverables will be taken up and mainstreamed into the outcomes of the Belem Declaration. Excellencies, Africa's priorities are clear. To accelerate progress towards the Paris Agreement targets and within the framework of the common but differentiated responsibility, the continent is determined to take bold steps. Among them is the establishment of an African climate facility and an African climate innovation compact, which are designed to mobilize $50 billion annually in a catalytic finance. This effort will help champion homegrown solutions, accelerate innovations, and scale climate action across communities. Equally important is our ambition to position Africa as a global hub for low carbon manufacturing and green intra-African trade by advancing along a green first pathway to economic growth. At the same time, the continent is committed to scaling up investment in renewable energy with a collective goal of reaching 300 gigawatts of installed capacity by 2030. This ambition is not only about reducing emissions, it is about creating jobs, ensuring universal energy access, and laying the foundation for a more resilient and inclusive economy. Africa also resolved to manage its mineral resources responsibly, particularly in critical minerals that are indispensable for sustainable growth and a just energy transition. The implementation of the African Green Mineral Strategy will be central to this. Furthermore, combating desertification and advancing land restoration remain high priorities. Programs such as the Great Green Wall the African Forest Landscape Restoration Initiative, Ethiopia's Green Legacy Initiative, and the Central Africa Forest Initiative provide concrete pathways for restoring degraded ecosystem and securing livelihoods. I would like to mention that we have spent close to $20 billion for the Ethiopian Green Legacy Initiative. This is indeed a bold measure and initiative that didn't wait other financers and contributors. Excellencies, food security also remains a pressing priority. The Addis Ababa Declaration called for tangible contribution in this area and for the implementation of the Secretary-General's appeal from the Addis Ababa UN Food Systems Stocktake Summit. Effective global solidarity is essential if we are to build a food secure and climate resilient future supported by the necessary financial resource and technological innovation. In this regard, I commend Brazil for the innovative measures it is pursuing through the Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty launched under its G20 presidency. Excellencies, finally, Africa extends an invitation to our friends. Walk with us. But our journey forward will never be dictated by the timid, nor constrained by the doubtful. The destiny of Africa rests in the hands of Africa, and our commitment is now. In Belem, Brazil, we will play our rightful role to bridge differences and foster new commitments and actionable targets. In this regard, we stand with our Brazilian brothers and sister to the successful hosting of the COP 30. And I thank you, Madam Chair.
I thank the President of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia. And our next speaker is His Excellency Luong Cuong, State President of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

Her her her her her her her her her her her her her her her her.

Distinguished delegates, I thank the Secretary-General for convening the special high event on climate action, a most important event that demonstrates the strong resolve of the United Nations and the international community to join hands in addressing climate change. Vietnam is among the developing countries most severely affected by climate change. We are very clearly aware of and remain steadfast in our pursuit of sustainable development goals. striving for a harmonious balance between economic growth, environmental protection, and climate change response. Vietnam has continuously improved its related institutions and policies and established a coherent legal framework that enables green and just transition, climate change adaptation, and strong and resolute actions to achieve committed goals alongside the international community. At the same time, Vietnam will also continue to enhance adaptive capacity and resilience in vulnerable areas and communities in regions affected by climate change so that no one is left behind. On this occasion, allow me to propose three key points. First, all countries in the international community need to ensure the full and timely delivery of climate finance commitments with particular attention to resources for a just transition. This process should be aligned with social security, job creation and support for vulnerable workers and communities. Second, we need to accelerate in more vigorous and substantive manner, the transfer of advanced, clean and efficient technologies to support the development of a green and circular economy, which will help developing countries to bridge the development gaps. Third, the United Nations must continue to play a central role in fostering solidarity, cooperation, trust building, and ensuring equity and justice, and in realizing the objectives of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement on the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Developed nations should take the lead in fulfilling their strong commitments to emissions reduction, finance, and technology contributions. They should also initiate and spread new initiatives and solutions, foster dialogues, and connect nations, businesses, social organizations, and citizens worldwide to collectively take actions. Thank you.
Of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. Our next speaker is Her Excellency Hilda Heine, President of the Republic of the Marshall Islands.

President Lula, Deputy Secretary-General, fellow leaders, distinguished participants, I bring warm greetings of from the Marshall Islands. I also bring a demand for us all to wake up. From communities whose hospitals and schools are being destroyed by king tides brought on by sea level rise, whose crops are being devastated by rising temperatures and the salination of our soil, by communities facing the prospect of migration from their homelands, I ask you to wake up. As the iAmbition Coalition said this morning, we cannot silence the science. The NDCs delivered so far do not keep 1.5 in reach. As the ICJ decided, 1.5 is legally binding. It is the only threshold under which countries like mine can keep our people safe and preserve our human rights. In my first week in office this term, my government was forced to declare national emergencies due to devastating flooding and droughts. If we fail to wake up now and end our dependence on fossil fuels, the leaders of every country in this room will be woken up by calls about catastrophes of wildfires, of storms, of heat waves, of starvation and drought, and the lives of our citizens lost as a result. The Marshall Islands is doing its part. We submitted our third nationally determined contribution in February. we committed to emissions reductions by at least 58% by 2035 compared to 2010 levels. Our NDC covers emissions across the country's economy and sets out a path for transitioning away from fossil fuels. In transport, we've drawn on our strong cultural heritage of navigation, to begin transforming our inter-island transport to a low-carbon future. We're strengthening traditional canoe building skills for transport inside our atoll lagoons, training young people in how to build these zero-carbon vessels. For longer inter-island transport needs, we've launched a state-of-the-art cargo hybrid sailing ship, the Juranai. which uses wind and solar energy to reduce emissions by 80%. Our NDC sets out not only how the country will rapidly cut its emissions, but also steps it will take to adapt and build resilience and respond to loss and damage as a result of the climate crisis. But plans on paper mean nothing without the finance to deliver it. We desperately need dedicated finance for adaptation and loss and damage. Fellow leaders, and especially those of you from the G20, if the Marshall Islands can deliver an ambitious NDC, so can you. In fact, as the ICJ decisions confirm, you are legally required to. you must deliver stronger NDCs that can meet 1.5 and say how you will transition away from fossil fuels. The opportunities for our economies and our people and planet's health far outweigh the short-term costs. A decade ago in Paris, the international community came together and offered the world hope. this year against the odds, we must do so again. I thank you.
I thank the President of the Republic of the Marshall Islands. Our next speaker is His Excellency Feleti Teo, Prime Minister of Tuvalu.

Thank you, Madam President. with all protocols duly observed. I thank the Secretary-General for convening this important event at a time when the world needs courage, clarity, and conviction. And it is indeed my greatest honor to share that Tuvalu has in the last couple of days announced its Nationally Determined Contribution, NDC 3.0. This is our strongest pledge yet to the Paris Agreement and to securing a livable future for Tuvalu and for all humankind. As we mark 10 years since the Paris Agreement, this is a defining moment for boldness. Through Tuvalu's NDC 3.0, we raise our ambition to the highest level, showing that even the smallest nation can lead because our survival and that of the planet is on the line. Tuvalu therefore commits to, one, achieving a 100% reduction of emissions from the electricity sector, moving to near zero power generation by 2030; two, cutting total emission from the energy sector by 80% below the 2014 levels by 2035, and free following a zero carbon development pathway by 2050. These will be achieved in a manner that is just and fair and respecting the rights and dignity of every Tuvaluan. Excellencies. Tuvalu's NDC 3.0 is ambitious because our survival demands nothing less, but we cannot act alone. Tuvalu therefore call on major emitters to, one, step up methane action with binding commitment, two, transition away from fossil fuel, three, honor climate finance promises for a just transition, and four, deliver new NDCs aligned with the 1.5 target ahead of the COP30 in Belm to be accompanied by robust implementation strategy. The ICJ advisory opinion on climate change has made it crystal clear that inaction is not just immoral, it is unlawful. Together, we must rise to the challenge of honoring both legal and moral responsibility in safeguarding our shared future and pulling the emergency brake on methanes. Cutting methane is the fastest scalable way to slow global warming, avoiding up to 0.3 degrees centigrade of warming by 2040 and buying critical time for long-term CO2 decarbonization strategies to take effect. The path ahead will not be without challenges, yet with political will and strengthened international cooperation, we can meet them. Let us commit not only to setting ambitious target, but to taking concrete action that ensure a safe and sustainable future for all. I thank you, Madam President.
I thank the Prime Minister of Tuvalu. Our next speaker is His Excellency Andrew Holness, Prime Minister of Jamaica.

Excellencies, I wish to extend Jamaica's support for the work of the COP presidency of Brazil and the UNFCCC ahead of COP30. Climate change is an existential threat to both the livelihoods and environments of communities worldwide, but disproportionately so to SIDS and LDCs. Sobering reports and assessments globally of the current state of the climate have increased the necessity for enhanced adaptation and mitigation measures to confront the challenges and bolster resilience. In Jamaica, the nation is contending with intensifying adverse effects of climate change. Droughts, floods, tropical storms, and hurricanes have already impeded Jamaica's development. 90% of our GDP is generated in close proximity to coastal regions. Robust adaptation measures are not merely preferable but are imperative. Over the past decade, Jamaica has made steady progress in climate action. Yet, as we know, global climate ambition remains below what is required. And countries like ours must lead with both credibility and innovation. Jamaica's journey with our nationally determined contributions reflect this leadership. Our first NDC focused primarily on the energy sector, targeting up to a 10% reduction in emissions. By 2020, Jamaica became the first Caribbean nation and the 11th globally to submit an updated NDC, increasing our ambition with targets of 25.4% unconditionally and 28% conditionally by 2030. We have also broadened our scope to include forestry and land use change, further strengthening our climate leadership. I am proud to announce that Jamaica submitted its further updated NDC 3.0, which is both comprehensive and realistic and further aligns our ambition with action. Jamaica's targets are anchored in existing policies and supported by political will. Key highlights of our NDC include a broader push for renewable electricity, energy efficiency in the water sector, and electric vehicle adoption, targeting 12% of private fleets and 16% of public fleets by 2030. decarbonization in the cement industry by 40 kilotons of CO2, and zero net loss of forest along with mangroves and seagrass restoration. Excellencies, by 2035, Jamaica aims for emission reductions between 26% and 41.7% compared to 2012 levels depending on the scale of international support received. Jamaica is producing an implementation plan for NDC 3.0 that will provide a clear roadmap with sector-specific targets, stakeholder responsibilities, and costing to guide investment and partnership. This is not just a pledge, it is a practical economy-wide strategy for a low-emission, climate-resilient future. In closing, Jamaica reaffirms its commitment as a party to the UNFCCC on climate change and the Paris Agreement. Jamaica remains dedicated to delivering on NDCs with increased ambitions for emissions reduction in mind, while also pursuing just transition, green growth, and a climate-resilient future for all. Jamaica welcomes the support of the international community as it pursues these ambitious goals. I thank you.
I thank the Prime Minister of Jamaica. And our next speaker is His Excellency Sadiq Zappah.

This includes financial projects in the area of ecology and sustainable development to regions, mountainous regions, through the Climate Trust Fund. We invite investors to participate in our green projects, dear participants, as a mountain country.
