I thank the President of the Kyrgyz Republic, and I would now like to welcome to the podium His Excellency William Samoei Ruto, President of the Republic of Kenya.

Excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, as we approach the 10th anniversary of the Paris Agreement, the political landscape has become more polarized and more uncertain. Yet the urgency of climate action has never been greater. This crisis, ladies and gentlemen, is accelerating with devastating consequences across sectors. It drives instability, weakens economies, and forces many countries to divert very scarce resources from health, education, and social protection into emergency responses. At COP13, Brazil, we must set the highest possible ambition for NDCs, firmly aligned with a 1.5 degrees pathway. That was the spirit of the second Africa Climate Summit, where Africa asserted its agency, spoke with one voice, and demanded that global commitments be honored. Kenya has already acted. Early this year, we submitted our NDC 3.0, bold, economy-wide, and grounded in a whole-of-society approach. Our targets are ambitious, but also hopeful. We offer global solutions for emission reductions at scale if adequate financing is provided. At the same time, endless debate continues over fossil fuel reserves, while our immense endowments in sunlight, wind, and geothermal lies underutilized. This, even as millions still lack electricity and clean cooking solutions. Economic growth, ladies and gentlemen, and climate action are inseparable. Ignore the climate, the development will unravel. Confront the crisis and new pathways for green inclusive growth open. That is why new, predictable and innovative financing must be unlocked. At COP28 in Dubai, building on the Africa declaration of Nairobi declaration, we launched the global solidarities levies task force. A fast breakthrough came this June when eight countries, including Kenya, formed a coalition to introduce solidarity levies on premium class flyers. These initiatives must inform the Baku to Belm roadmap to mobilize the 1.3 trillion that developing countries urgently need. Africa is already stepping up. At this year's Africa Climate Summit, eight leading African financial institutions signed a cooperation framework to unlock US dollars 100 billion in investment capital. At the same time, When the world risks fragmentation and a retreat into transactional politics, Africa is leaning forward to shape its own destiny. We now invite the global community to join us, to stand with us in this noble undertaking. This is the moment to be bolder, to show genuine climate solidarity, and to silence the naysayers. I thank you for your attention.
I thank the President of the Republic of Kenya. Our next speaker is Her Excellency Dina Ersilia Bularte Zegarra, President of the Republic of Peru.

I thank you and good afternoon, everyone. Peru is one of the countries with the greatest degree of biodiversity in the world, thanks to the 39 ecosystems that we have identified throughout our territory. More than 60% of our territory is covered by the Amazon, and we have 68% of tropical glaciers of the world. However, In the last 58 years, climate change has led to the loss of 56% of our total area, affecting the cycle of water at the Amazon, and our ocean as well is suffering from warming and acidification. and this has an impact on the livelihoods of our population. Even though less than 0.5% of global emissions come from Peru, we are highly vulnerable to climate change, and that is why we are calling for a comprehensive climate action which includes effective adaptation accelerated mitigation as well as sustainable development. And at this crucial moment for the world, Peru reaffirms its commitment to the Paris Agreement through the updating of our NDCs that we have called NDC 3.0. And it will be presented during COP30 in Belem in Brazil. Our NDC 3.0 will reflect a renewed ambition towards a resilient future, which will be low in carbon, and this will be done through a participatory process with indigenous peoples, local governments, regional governments, the private sector, and civil society. and mitigation by 2035. Here, we commit to not go beyond the 179 tons of carbon dioxide. We have 76 measures aimed at decarbonization in five sectors, energy, transportation, agriculture, waste, and forests. In adaptation, we prioritize territorial measures in seven areas, water, forests, agriculture, health, fisheries, and agriculture, tourism, and transportation. And we have incorporated migration and green jobs, totaling 84 measures, as well as a component on loss and damage. Peru is ready to take part in comprehensive approaches according to Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. with a national registry of mitigation measures which facilitate investment in decarbonization. Peru is showing that climate action is possible only through political will, respect for multilateralism, and international cooperation. In this way, we can accelerate the solutions for climate change, taking care of our own home, our only home, Earth, Pachamama. Thank you.
I thank the President of the Republic of Peru. Our next speaker is His Majesty King Mswati III, Head of State of the Kingdom of Eswatini.

Madam Moderator, Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, distinguished ladies and gentlemen, It is an honor to address this gathering as climate change threatens humanity and the planet. The Kingdom of Swaziland supports climate action despite our low greenhouse gas emissions. We are highly impacted by climate change, including droughts, floods, landslides, and strong winds, which contributes to the national development burden of adaptation. Despite this, Eswatini comes to this meeting determined to turn vulnerability into resilience. We are pleased to announce that we have concluded and submitted the Paris Agreement compliant NDC 3.0 to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The Kingdom is among the 10 African countries that met the September 22nd deadline, a significant milestone, thanks to the support of the local UN office and partners. The NDC 3.0 revision process was comprehensive and inclusive, with the greenhouse gas data local driven, providing that we own the process. In forming the process were lessons from NDC 2.0 and meaningful dialogues that produced a powerful, inclusive report. The report aligns with the 2023-28 National Development Plan, the first National Adaptation Plan, and the Long-Term Low Emissions Development Strategy. Eswatini will reform laws and strengthen all institutions to improve capacity, accountability, monitoring, and reporting. Financial constraint prevented NDC 2.0 from meeting its $900 million to $1.5 billion target. Eswatini has only raised about $449 million since 2018. The NDC 3.0, estimated to cost over $2.4 billion U.S., requires scaled up and predictable climate change and predictable climate finance. Thus, we expect stronger collaboration with our partners, including the local private sector, to finance the $2 billion U.S. gap. Eswatini will remain a net carbon sink and reduce 2.24 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions by 2035. We will also invest in climate smart agriculture and technology. Early warning systems, water resource management, waste management, and infrastructure will be improved to protect our most vulnerable society. The just energy transition will promote affordable clean technologies and a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy. Our green finance instruments and incentives align financial flows with climate priorities and attract sustainable investment. To improve risk financing and reporting, we have created a Sendai-aligned disaster risk management fund while continuing to promote renewable energy and digital tools. Technology and capacity building partnerships will accelerate the green and low carbon transition. It is important that finance must match talent and drive. Climate smart technologies should be affordable for farmers homeowners and entrepreneurs after the loss and damage fund is recapitalized. We must all consider innovative internal and external resource mobilization strategies to unlock capital for adaptation and resilience. Otherwise, the Paris Agreement may break its promises. Finally, improving global financial architecture is essential for Eswatini's NDC 3.0 goals. Madam President, about survival and the opportunity, with the right support, Eswatini can turn climate challenges into green growth, food sovereignty, and shared prosperity. I thank you. May almighty God bless us all.
I thank you. Majesty King Mswati, Head of State of Kingdom of Eswatini. Our next speaker is His Excellency Emmanuel Macron, President of the French Republic.

Thank you very much. Distinguished chairs, heads of state and government, ministers, ambassadors, All protocols observed. I will try to get to the brass tacks as quickly as possible because here we all know full well why we're gathered here today. Almost 10 years ago, the Paris Agreement set our common objectives underpinned by science, and I'll get to that later. Across all latitudes of our planet, we see that the consequences of climate change are self-evident And this is all the more clearer today, 10 years on. France, since 2017, has been complying with its carbon budget, and we're living up to our obligations. We're going to continue doing that. You can count on our economy. You can count on our country. My second takeaway is that we must also rise to the occasion at the end of 2025. We know that there are going to be a number of objectives. which we must meet at the COP30 in Belm, and that's very important. And I'd like to express our support to President Lula, all of the negotiators. You have our support. Let's keep it simple. Europeans will be there in Belm, living up to expectations, and France will be defending that meeting. We'll be going down our 2050 carbon neutral climate path. We'll be submitting our nationally determined contribution, our NDCs, underpinned by science, bringing together private and public investment in accordance with the trajectory we've set. And on that note, France supports the establishment of interstate carbon credits, which will be a way of going further, as well as other mechanisms which will allow us to assist our industries as they undergo this transition, making them able to get there. That's what we'll be submitting before the end of the year by November in Belem at the COP30. Aside from the NDCs, I wanted to talk about some of the key goals coming up in the next few months against this context. Progressive phase out of fossil energies. This is something we decided on in Dubai. This is absolutely vital and that's why we need to accelerate our efforts, moving away from carbon in particular. we need to think about previous COPs as we look ahead to the future. So we've established mechanisms to fund this transition, to address the issue of investments that were recently made, so that no one says it'll be a good idea to reopen up carbon-heavy industries. Instead of doing that, instead of backsliding, we need to accelerate the transition. This was said by a previous speaker. We need binding objectives on methane. We know that this is a reachable goal, and we participate. We are participating in the Global Methane Pledge, bringing together 150 countries. I encourage those who haven't yet done so to join our ranks. This is the best way to reduce our emissions, and it's also a G7 priority. We'll be chairing the G7. next year. My third takeaway I wanted to underscore is ecosystem restoration. We know, thanks to the work of the IPCC and IPBES, that there are deep synergies between our fight to limit CO2 emissions and the fight for biodiversity, they're mutually reinforcing. Therefore, and I don't want to take up too much of your time, but that's why we need to forthfully fight to protect our oceans and our primary forests, because these two fights are part and parcel of our efforts to protect biodiversity. Three quarters of the world's biodiversity are located in those primary forests. We have a lot of biodiversity, a wealth of biodiversity in our oceans. So, to protect those primary forests and oceans, they're remarkable carbon sinks. in particular those contained in our primary forests. So we're going to continue taking action on forests. The Belém meeting will be important as we will be hosting up our commitment to the Amazon. France is one of the countries of the Amazon. We have French Guyana, which is located in the Amazon. So we'll be proposing new financing mechanisms so as to further protect the Amazon. Now, we shouldn't We shouldn't forget about Southeast Asia and the Pacific. Think about what's happening in the PNG, in Papua New Guinea, and Africa as well. There are forests there. That's a key objective. Therefore, everything we're going to be deploying, those country packages are absolutely vital if we are to help preserve these forests. We are putting so much money into reforestation, but we also need to preserve existing forests. We're not doing that enough. We need Those countries which have those forests, they might be losing out on economic opportunities by keeping these forests in the ground. So we need for the international community to help those countries. We also want to mention the Nice conference. An enormous collective effort was undertaken. I'd like to thank the UN, all of our partners, something that was spearheaded by us and our friends, Costa Rica. We exceeded the 60% ratification threshold for the BBNJ Treaty. So great progress, but we need to strengthen collective work, protect the high seas. Thanks to the BBNJ, we're now going to be working on implementation of that. The 30-30 Montreal objective. exclusive economic areas, protecting them. And I'd also like to invite you in so much as possible to join the deep sea mining moratorium. That's absolutely essential if we are to preserve biodiversity. So we need to revitalize our efforts. to protect oceans and forests. Also, the fight for financing, an important endeavor for Belem as well. The EU is taking action. We are the world's top donor. 28 billion euros were pledged. That's a quarter of the world's climate finance. France, together with the French Development Agency, is mobilizing 7 billion euros for climate action. We've tripled Our commitment over the last decade will continue to mobilize on international finance. Last but not least, aside from all these timelines, all of this action, what we want to be doing at Belem, the NDCs, and what I just mentioned, we must also continue this method, implementing this method, bringing everyone together, bringing together scientists, governments, companies, and NGOs. This method, part and parcel of it, is the Pact for People and Prosperity, the 4Ps, which brings together 73 states and has come up with innovative initiatives thanks to this mobilization. I'll just mention a few. Kenya, Barbados, Spain, Somalia, Sierra Leone, Antigua and Barbuda, the list goes on. Many countries have committed to improvements in aviation, resilience, innovative financing, that's what it's called. We need to continue forging coalitions to mobilize innovative financing. With the UK, we've created a framework for biodiversity credits and essential mechanisms to achieve what I just mentioned on forests. Pilot projects have already been crafted. We have robust methodology so that we don't repeat the mistakes of the past with carbon credits. We also need to further take into consideration climate vulnerability when allocating development bank financing, and that's the 4P reform, reforming the big banks. To achieve this, we need to keep in mind a few simple principles. No country should have to choose between combating poverty and protecting the planet. Every country should be able to choose their own path. We need to increase fundings funneled to the most vulnerable countries. It's a matter of justice, and it's these countries, these countries which are suffering the most from climate change. We need to mobilize private finance a lot more. That's at the heart of the World Bank and the IMF reforms. This is necessary to ensure we achieve this transition. And last but not least, science should be at the heart of our policies, of the decisions we take. Sometimes we hear narratives to the effect that climate issues, biodiversity, are up for debate. Some people say the science is not clear cut, but I do believe the science is clear. Recognized scientists, eminent scientists, harbor no doubts. We defend open, free science so that we can underpin our decisions with that science and that is why 800 IPCC scientists will be meeting later this year to continue driving ahead this agenda here at the United Nations so that we make good decisions. Thank you very much for your collective efforts. I thank you.
I thank the President of the French Republic and now welcome His Excellency, Tshering Tobgay, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Bhutan.

I thank the Secretary General for convening this important event and President Lula for his leadership as we prepare for COP30. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I am honored to present a preview from Bhutan's third Nationally Determined Contribution, our enhanced commitment under the Paris Agreement. Bhutan is already carbon negative. absorbing five times more carbon dioxide than we emit, and over 70% of our land is under forest cover. We are determined to stay that way, even as we pursue sustainable growth, tackle poverty, and improve livelihoods. NDC 3.0 sets clear, quantifiable goals for 2035, and is integrated into our 10X economic roadmap and our updated long-term low emission strategy. At its heart lies the Guelphu Mindfulness City, a bold model for low emission, climate resistance, urban development. But our commitment come at a real cost. We forgo hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue every year by not exploiting our natural resources. We spend 3.2% of our GDP on climate and biodiversity, which is among the highest in the world today. We subsidize rural electricity to reduce firewood use and have embedded climate education in our education system. Yet, the effects of the climate crisis are escalating. To cite but just one example, road restoration costs due to climate impact have risen by 112%, diverting much needed funds for urgent development works. Bhutan is doing more than its fair share, but we cannot do it alone. We call on the international community for predictable finance, technology, and capacity support so that we can sustain our neutrality and resilience. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, we want COP30 to be the implementation COP, where ambition is translated into delivery. Bhutan will lead by example, submitting NDC 3.0 ahead of COP30 with concrete, actionable targets. Projects like the Gelephu Mindfulness City and our REDD+ initiatives show how even a small, vulnerable nation can pioneer solutions anchored in nature and regenerative development. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I am pleased to announce here that we will launch our NDC 3.0 in Lyar, a nomadic highland community. The village is situated at over 4,000 meters above sea level. By doing so, we highlight the frontline of climate change, melting glaciers, risks of glacial lake outburst floods, biodiversity loss, degraded pastures, and rising human-wildlife conflict. Highland communities all over the world, like Laya, are already living the consequences of climate change and need us to act on their behalf urgently. The time for rhetoric is over. Let us act decisively together. Thank you for your kind attention and Teshidila.
I thank the Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Bhutan. Our next speaker is His Excellency **** Schoof, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

Esteemed colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, we are now 10 years on since Paris Agreement.

Ten years of working hard nationally and internationally to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees. I think it's fair to say that much has been achieved, but not enough. We need to pick up the pace as we remain committed to tackling climate change together. Only with a collective level of ambition equal to the scale of the challenge will we be able to deliver a sustainable future for all. More action and more international cooperation is essential. to ensure a livable environment and to secure livelihoods for today's generation and for many generations to come. At the same time, the green transition offers enormous opportunities for attracting investment and stimulating trade in renewable energy, water management, and food security. For us in the Netherlands, climate change and green growth are two sides of the same coin. And as we discussed, the nationally determined contributions on our way to Belem I think we should focus on the second word. We must stay determined. And I assure you, Europe and the Netherlands are determined. Our compliments to all the parties that already have published their new NDCs. We know how much effort has gone into this. EU is preparing a joint NDC so that it can be submitted ahead of the COP30. Our emissions reduction targeted for 2035 will be in keeping with the proposed target for 2040, that will eventually be enshrined in law. As you know, and as you've heard from the Chair of the Commission, the European Commission has proposed a target of 90%. In a union with 27 member states, it's important to allow the democratic process to run its course. We will be in time for Belem, and we will not disappoint the world. Setting targets is the first step. Implementing them is second. And it's only fair to admit that when we talk about a green transition, other interests are at stake as well. So we need to keep a realistic view, a realistic pace, and a realistic discussion because we need everybody, everyone, people and business on board. And I'm happy to tell that the Kingdom of the Netherlands is definitely on board. We offer a world-class knowledge and expertise in areas such as water management, climate smart agriculture, and renewable energy, such as green hydrogen. And we stand ready to work together with other countries and institutions through knowledge sharing, technology transfer, capacity building, and innovative forms of finance. Together, we must close the implementation gap and accelerate the green transition. In conclusion, to reach the outcomes of the global stocktake, we need to be determined. Determined in our commitment to follow through on the agreement we made 10 years ago, and determined to implement our NDCs together. Let us move forward at a faster pace, and let us reaffirm our deep commitment to the Paris Agreement. Thank you.
I thank the Prime Minister of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Our next speaker is His Excellency Pedro Sanchez Perez Castillon, President of the Government of Spain.

I thank you very much, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Devastating fires have affected Spain this past winter. Almost 400,000 hectares have burned so far this year. And it's more than a dozen states of the United Nations. However, the data is undeniable. And this has been the hottest summer since we've kept records. And the climate emergency is moving forward. And yet the ambition to face it, unfortunately, is backsliding. And this is unacceptable because we have to comply with what we agreed upon and we have to present a new round of NDCs in line with the objective of 1.5 degrees centigrade because our lives depend on it. And we have to redirect the course and the COP30 in Belem is the place to do it. Spain is working with all of the other European partners in order to present an NDC at the European level in line with science and with the objective of reducing 90% of emissions by 2040. We have to move decisively. We can't backslide. And my country is working in three priority areas with respect to climate action, which I would like to share with you now. First of all, financing. We must continue to make concrete steps when it comes to financing to be credible in the fight against climate change. The Sabil commitment and the Sabil platform for actions adopted in the fourth financing for development conference represents a milestone in strengthening international financing. And secondly, the fight against misinformation and disinformation. Disinformation does not only create confusion, it spreads false news, and in the framework of the climate emergency, it places at risk lives and property. And that is why climate disinformation as well is an actor that kills. And today, I'd like to announce that Spain supports the Global Initiative for Informational Integrity on Climate Change. Because it's not simply fighting hoaxes, it's about saving lives. And lastly, and in last place, improving our prevention systems in the light of extreme climate phenomena, which unfortunately will be more frequent and more violent. And this is the reason behind the proposal that I'm making to all of the institutions and this Danish civil society, all of the political parties, to agree on a great state pact in the light of climate change. because the threat that we are facing doesn't recognize ideologies, nor does it stop at borders. And that is why fighting the climate emergency is not an abstract idea. Unfortunately, our citizens, all of us, we must every day face this climate change that is advancing. It's a matter of protecting our houses, our jobs, it's protecting our way of life. Climate change not only kills, it also impoverishes our societies. And if some, for ideological reasons that have nothing to do with science, if they don't feel affected by this, well, at least they should motivate themselves for other people. Thank you.
I thank the President of Spain for his statement. Our next speaker is His Excellency Luis Alberto Arce Catacora, Constitutional President of the Plurinational State of Bolivia.

Thank you very much. Good afternoon, everyone, Excellencies, and all of those who are here. The paradigm, the Western capitalist paradigm, and through postcentric has placed humankind in the greatest challenge to its history, the climate crisis, creating a reality where, paradoxically, developing countries who are not the ones who are guilty of this, we suffer the most serious impacts. All of the countries must assume their commitments to live well in harmony and in balance with Mother Earth. and within the framework of the principles of equity and common but shared responsibilities. Developed countries that have greater responsibilities, historic responsibilities, must take leadership when it comes to resolving the climate crisis and guarantee financing, technology transfer, as well as capacity building for developing countries. The main message of the developed countries that we have heard at this summit must be to achieve carbon neutrality by the latest by the year 2035. One real solution to the climate crisis also has to include the commitment of the United States, the country with the largest global historic emissions, to comply with their climate obligations within the framework of the Paris Agreement. Greenhouse gas emissions in Bolivia are minimal, but we assume our responsibility within the context of the Paris Agreement, and we have presented our NDC. 3.0. However, without climate financing and means of implementation, our commitments will not be able to become a reality. Without a fair transition, an international transition, actions in our countries will always be inequitable and will be limited in achieving our right to development. Bolivia is a victim of the unjust energy transition. Bolivia has drastically reduced its production of fossil fuels and with the lack of a just transition of being an exporting country, now we're importing fossil fuels and we have to devote more resources to pay for the external debt. As a result, there are not global conditions for a just energy transition. Today, Bolivia can affirm that we have taken a historic step forward. On the 15th of July this year, our program for emission reductions due to deforestation promoted by the indigenous government of Charagua and Gambay in our country, it was certified in the UN platform, placing us in the carbon international market with credits of high integrity and indigenous leadership. This milestone not only makes visible the climate vision of the country, but it also shows that we have laid the basis to exceed to climate financing, complying with three of the five conditions, and consolidating state capabilities and community capabilities. With vast forest areas and a potential for mitigation and also social benefits, our model can be replicated at the national level, especially in protected areas, in order to ensure effective protection. We have a registry of programs and projects along these lines, which are being fully developed, and we are moving forward in consolidating them with other management instruments. We are strengthening the protection information systems to guarantee transparency rights. And we will develop a mechanism to redistribute benefits, which is both just and transparent, which favors those who protect forests. We invite international cooperation as well as markets to accompany these sovereign efforts. Bolivia is ready to use measurable results, results of integrity, which would protect the Amazon as well as our entire ecosystem, generating well-being for our peoples and contributing concretely to the global goal of limiting global warming. We have assumed as a country the commitment to carry out significant and drastic reductions in deforestation of the Amazon by 2030 and strengthening the comprehensive conservation of our forests. However, without the provision of financing today and now, this task will be impossible. And that is why we would like to say that the fund for forests led by Brazil, and which will be launched in COP30, this should incorporate the provision of early resources and advanced resources for future results. We welcome the fact that Brazil would be the seat of COP30 in Belem. an emblematic symbol of the Amazon, convinced that multilateralism is the only path to overcome the climate emergency, and that in this COP, the leadership of Brazil will protect the interests of developing countries. Thank you very much.
I thank the constitutional president of Bolivia. Our next speaker is His Excellency Jeremiah Manela, Prime Minister of the Solomon Islands.

Co-chairs, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, we gather here today at a time when the impacts of climate change continue to define our shared future. Solomon Islands is positioned in a location where the impact of climate change is three times the global average. Climate change is a daily reality. Eroding coastlines, sea level rise, biodiversity loss, and the frequency and intensity of disasters is placing stress on our people, economy, and livelihoods. We face a climate emergency that is not of our making. The NDCs are the cornerstone of the Paris Agreement that can place us on a 1.5 degree Celsius pathway. We are here today to renew our commitment to our people with ambitious climate action. Solomon Islands has done more than its fair share in submitting an ambitious third cycle net positive nationally determined contribution, NDC commitment. Allow me to briefly explain. Our greenhouse gas emissions peaked in 2018 at 861.5 kilotons of carbon dioxide equivalent, excluding removals. Under a business as usual trajectory, our emissions was supposed to increase by 2% by 2035. However, our standing forests is removing greenhouse gases about 30 times more than our combined national greenhouse gas emissions. We are already net positive and determined to strengthen our net positive status. Our ambition can further be enhanced by 17% with new and additional international support in the form of finance, technology transfer, and capacity building. Ladies and gentlemen, our forests serve as carbon sink and currently absorbing approximately 26.3 million tons of carbon dioxide annually. With investments in reforestation and forest conservation, we have the potential to cut emissions by a further 34% reducing projected 2035 emissions to around 798,000 tons per year. In closing, Solomon Islands urge all parties, especially major emitters, those with historical responsibility, to submit new, more ambitious NDCs that are aligned with the 1.5 degree Celsius pathway. COP30 in Belm is opportunity for a recourse. Ambition delayed is 1.5 degree Celsius pathway denied. We must act now with ambition. I thank you for your attention.
I thank the Prime Minister of the Solomon Islands. Our next speaker is His Excellency Alexander Van der Bellen, Federal President of the Republic of Austria.

Thank you.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, we are all seeing the writing on the wall. The temperature increase that is being recorded, plus 1.6 degrees Celsius globally, plus 3.1 degrees in Austria, double the global increase of temperature. The glaciers in Austria are disappearing. Then the wildfires, for instance, in Spain and Portugal, the floods, among others, in Austria one year ago, the rising sea levels threatening small island states in the Pacific. But there are positive messages, too, some small, some bigger. Looking at my own country, Austria, I noticed that for the third consecutive year, the greenhouse gas emissions of Austria have decreased, summing up to a reduction of around 14%. Where there is a will, there is a way, and there is a will in Austria. We do take measures, bigger and smaller ones. For one, we support the presentation of the EU member states' joint NDCs at the COP30 in Belm. Secondly, we are currently finalizing a new climate law, laying the groundwork for our ambition to achieve climate neutrality by 2040, 10 years ahead of the EU's climate target. Thirdly, we will install a new governance structure, including a mechanism to involve state and non-state actors and an advisory board of climate and other scientists. And we have introduced the so-called climate check, ensuring that climate policies are mainstreamed across all sectors of policymaking. The energy transition is in full speed in Austria. On top of our already existing hydropower capacity, there's a rapidly growing wind and solar energy sector, every day taking us a step further towards our goal of 100% green power generation by 2030. And yes, like so many other countries, we also face budgetary constraints. But inaction would end up being far more expensive than investing now in a climate-neutral economy, which is why Austria will continue to contribute appropriately to international climate finance and is actively engaged in the UN climate and security mechanism. Ladies and gentlemen, many other bigger and smaller positive messages are around the corner of some of them we have heard today. And I hope that COP30 in Belem will witness an ambitious coalition of member states willing and ready to change course Austria will be there standing with you. Thank you for your attention.
I thank the Federal President of the Republic of Austria. Our next speaker is His Excellency Americo Ramos, Prime Minister of the Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and Principe.

Excellencies, heads of state, distinguished delegates, It is a great honor and with great sense of responsibility that I direct my words to this illustrious audience in the name of the people and the government of the Republic Democratic of Sao Tome and Principe. In spite of us having a small area, we reaffirm our commitment to the global response to the climate problem. We are naturally a carbon sink due to the richness of our ecosystems, which cover more than half of our national territory. Nonetheless, we don't limit ourselves to that role. We reaffirm our ambition of net zero as delineated in our national decarbonization plan and reflected in our NDCs 3.0, which will be officially presented before COP30. Allow me to highlight some central measures of our NDC 3.0. We have increased the NDC 2.0 goals for reducing emissions to 27% to 36% by 2035 based on the national inventory of 2018. We have committed to increase the participation of the share of renewables in our grid to up to 50% by 2035, along with robust efficiency measures. NDC 3.0 places adaptation at the center of our activities as far as infrastructure, tourism, biodiversity are concerned, trying to quantify for the first time the costs of adaptation measures. We are strengthening our efforts, including gender equality and including the youth in our efforts. Excellencies, as far as in the name of ecological protection, we are passing law 820, which will prohibit the production of plastic bags, an important measure to end pollution by plastics. We have a national strategy of transitioning us to a blue economy with a plan to make these strategic goals real. We are also renewing our third national plan and strategy for biodiversity, as well as our biodiversity financial plan, to try to reverse the loss of biodiversity and thus guarantee the resiliency of our ecosystems. Our country is ready to explore high-impact initiatives, including the technical -- the Santiago Network to try to deal with losses and damages. We are committed, but we also realize that we will never reach these goals by ourselves. In this context, we realize the Secretary -- we acknowledge the Secretary of the Secretary-General and especially through the climate promise. Sao Tome and Principe is benefiting from technical, the UNDPs, the FAOs, and many other entities who are collaborating with this. We call for all our partners, be they government, private, or from civil society, that they redouble their efforts to reach the ambitious goals of and NDC 3.0 so that we can have concrete results. Together, we can guarantee that small island states and developing states, in spite of their vulnerabilities, can be leader in climate action and can be an example for the rest of the world. Thank you very much.
The Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and Principe. Our next speaker is His Excellency John Brizeno, Prime Minister of Belize.

Thank you very much, co-chairs and excellencies. Belize reaffirms our commitment, our unwavering commitment to the Paris Agreement and the 1.5 degree goal. 1.5 is not an aspiration. It is a threshold between hope and hardship, between flourishing communities and forced displacement, between shared prosperity and irreversible loss. Since our first nationally determined contribution in 2016, we have consistently raised our ambition. Today, our NDC 3.0 charts an even bolder course. strengthening our 2030 targets, and for the first time, setting 2035 target goals aligned with our long-term low emission development strategy. Our NDC 3.0 delivers concrete action, expanding renewable electricity generation from 53% to cover 75% of domestic needs by 2030, and 80% by 2035. by 2035, restoring 25,000 hectares of degraded forest and implementing sustainable land management on 90,000 hectares, or 3% of our land territory by 2030, doubling our carbon sequestration from 2.5 million tons in 2030 to 5.1 million tons in 2035, protecting and restoring 2.5 thousand hectares of mangroves while safeguarding an additional 8,000 hectares. Since submitting NDC 3.0, my government has committed to plant a million trees by 2028. Belize's NDCs 3.0 is expanding marine biodiversity protecting and protection to cover 30% of Belize's ocean by 2026, and driving emissions reductions across energy, waste, and agriculture. But let me be clear, ambition can only succeed if matched by support. For small climate vulnerable nations like Belize, this means scale up, predictable finance, accessible technology, and genuine partnerships. The science is unforgiving. The window for 1.5 degrees Celsius is closing rapidly. Belize will continue to lead with ambition, but the success of our NDC 3.0 and the global goal of 1.5 degrees Celsius depends on all of us acting with unprecedented urgency, solidarity, and climate justice. Thank you.
The next speaker is His Excellency Faustin-Archange Touadja, President of the Central African Republic.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor and a great responsibility for me to speak on behalf of the Central African Republic here in this Chamber, where the future of humanity hangs in the balance. My country, located in the heart of Africa, portrays the brutal reality of climate change, drought, flooding, deforestation, biodiversity loss. All of the above are intensifying year in, year out, making people already poverty-stricken more vulnerable, people who are suffering food insecurity and humanitarian crises. The Central African Republic, although it's one of the smallest emitters of greenhouse gases, is paying a disproportionate price through the crises which we didn't contribute to. This situation compels us to take the floor to recall that climate justice and global solidarity should be turned into deeds instead of simply remaining good intentions. Excellencies, we know that the world has fallen behind. Two months remain before the COP30. Only 40-odd countries, however, have submitted their renewed NDCs. And this despite the fact that scientists are recalling the urgency of maintaining the 1.5 degrees objective. The big emitters responsible for 80% of emissions have not yet submitted responses in keeping with the challenges we face. Piecemeal solutions are insufficient. History shows that we can undergo transformation, and the COP is an opportunity for us to deliver measurable results, to deliver results for our people. The Africa region is taking action with the support of the World Bank and the Global Environment Fund. We have launched the project aimed at promoting resilient infrastructure. This project is nature-based. It will strengthen urban resilience in Beberati and Bangui. Specifically, it will benefit 300,000 people. It will create 3.5 thousand green jobs, especially for women and young people. That's what it means, moving from commitments to results. Furthermore, we have a national strategy for the sustainable management of 7 million hectares, which are well protected, and some of them on the UNESCO Intangible Heritage List. It's not just about conservation. This is our direct contribution to striking a global climate equilibrium. Ladies and gentlemen, in September of last year, in Addis Ababa, at the African Summit, the African Climate Summit, Africa spoke with one voice. Accelerating climate solutions and financing for green and resilient development is what we called for. The Central African Republic is unswervingly committed to the above. We are promoting homegrown, inclusive solutions that are rooted in our communities. We are calling for equitable, direct and streamlined access to climate financing, climate financing, which is currently inaccessible and far too complex for vulnerable countries. We also want to swiftly see the operationalization of the loss and damage fund so that frontline countries can address the disasters threatening their very survival. Our ambition is clear cut. We want resilient green cities. We want to use nature to protect us. to ensure that we can resist climate shocks. We want to build low carbon economies that generates jobs and hope for our young people. We want climate governance that's equitable and inclusive, in which all citizens become agents of the transition. However, to get there, we need much more than pronouncements. We need climate integrity, consistency between what we say here and what we do back in our countries. Excellencies, partners, history is looking at what we do. Any delays, any missed deadlines results in lives lost, in generations sacrificed. The Central African Republic would like to reiterate our commitment to being a resolute actor of the fight for our climate. And we'd like to underscore that a fight waged by one country is not enough. What is called for is real operational global solidarity. We do not have the right to be indifferent. We no longer have the right to the status quo. We have a shared but differentiated responsibility. through which we can transform this crisis into an opportunity, an opportunity to build a fair, low-carbon, and sustainable future for all. Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your kind attention.
Thank you, Central African Republic. The next speaker is His Excellency Gaston Browne, Prime Minister of Antigua and Barbuda.

Thank you very much, co-chair, distinguished ladies and gentlemen, colleagues. For small island developing states, global decarbonization is not optional. It is a matter of justice. For over a century, the fossil fuel economy concentrated wealth and power in a few nations and industries. Those who profited most should now shoulder the cost of rapid, orderly, and fair transition. This is the polluter pays principle in action. Antigua and Barbuda has endorsed the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative to create a rules-based phase-out of coal, oil, and gas, backed by finance and technology. Climate change is a threat multiplier. It magnifies every vulnerability and accelerates every injustice. The farmer without irrigation loses his crop entirely. The fisher without insurance loses his boat and livelihood. Meanwhile, the large polluters rebuild and even expand. Across the Caribbean, the Pacific, and Africa, loss and damage is not a projection. It is our daily reality. For SIDS, holding a line at 1.5 degrees is non-negotiable. It is quintessential to our survival. Science confirms that fossil fuel emissions are contributing to climate change and that an overshoot of the 1.5 degrees will trigger irreversible damage. Law, to include the advisory opinions, tell us that it is a binding benchmark not a bargaining chip. Morality tells us that we cannot abandon it. Every fraction of a degree beyond 1.5 multiplies injustice. Stronger storms, higher seas, deeper loss and damage. Attribution science proves that the consequences of floods, storms, droughts, heat waves, and sea level rise destroying our countries are a direct consequence of emissions. emissions that we did not create. Attribution science also provides the evidence to hold the large polluters accountable. And I say to this august body that if diplomacy fails, then we should use the courts to hold these large polluters accountable. Without the attribution science, loss and damage risk would be dismissed as charity rather than recognized as responsibility. The global finance system remains unfit for purpose. IFIs and multilateral banks are not as responsive as they ought to be. Adaptation, for example, will cost up to 387 billion US dollars annually, and loss and damage already runs in the hundreds of billions. However, the climate funding for adaptation and mitigation remains grossly inadequate, And there is little funding available to fuel the urgent transition needed. Fairness demands equitable participation in the transition to include access to quality technologies, durable, efficient, low-carbon solutions at cost comparable to fossil fuels, protection from unfair burdens, finance at scale, that is concessional financing, primarily non-debt creating flows for renewable energy, clean transport, and resilient infrastructure. And it also requires capacity building, that is investments in people and institutions to sustain a net zero future. Colleagues, Antigua and Barbuda's National Adaptation Plan charts a clear path, and our updated NDC this year will move us closer to a green, resilient future. From survival to justice, that is our call today. Let us treat the 1.5 degree limit as a lifeline, not as a line in the sand. Let us make the polluter pays principle the foundation of a fair transition. And let us act not tomorrow, but today, so that the smallest and most vulnerable nations among us are not left to face the greatest storms alone. Finally, Let us continue to fight to accelerate the transition to renewables in protecting our planet and certainly in the interests of all of humanity. I thank you.
Thank you, Antigua and Barbuda. The next speaker is His Excellency Sitiveni Liga Mamata Rabuka, Prime Minister of the Republic of Fiji.

Co-Chair, Excellencies, I apologize for the very long name. It is an honor to address you today and to present the content of Fiji's third NDC. Fiji's revised NDC response with the appropriate scale of actions and across its element demonstrates a leveling up of our vision and our commitment. Fiji has pledged to increase our energy sector emissions reduction the reduction target from 30 to 36 percent. Your Excellencies, ONDC is our prospectus to support access to the means of implementation, the finance and technology, and the expertise required to supplement our resources. Fiji is firmly committed to harnessing indigenous forms of energy and the phasing out of fossil fuel use. We also target to produce 100 percent of our electricity from renewable energy sources by 2035. Fiji's revised NDC is more than a requirement under the Paris Agreement. Realistically, the scale of our nation's goals and their achievability depend heavily on the NDCs and the actions of major global players and emitters. The ICJ advisory opinion confirmed that states have a binding obligation to act in line with science, fairness, and equity. Large polluters must take responsibility, substantial and rapid and sustainable measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The advisory was also clear Non-proliferation of fossil fuels should be a priority in order to keep within the 1.5 degrees Celsius goal. COP30 in Belm must be the turning point with ambitious yet feasible NCDs. Sorry, NDCs. I urge my fellow leaders, you ladies and gentlemen, to take courage with the political will, the resources, and relentless drive to do what is right, what is right for humanity, for a sustainable future for all of us. Thank you very much.
Thank you, Republic of Fiji. The next speaker is His Excellency Alar Karis, President of the Republic of Estonia.

Thank you, Co-Chair, honored colleagues, ladies and gentlemen. Climate change is the greatest challenge of our time. It destroys homes, livelihoods, and ecosystems while fueling instability and insecurity. COP30 in Brazil must be a turning point with strong action plans aligned with the Paris Agreement. Ten years after its adoption, we now see real progress in clean technologies, competitive industries, and opportunities for a just transition. Excellencies, Estonia is fully committed to climate neutrality by 2050 and to multilateral climate cooperation. We have already reduced emissions by 63% compared to 1990, showing our determination to meet future goals. As part of EU, our NDC for COP30 reflects with strong commitment and responsibility to secure our nature and climate. Tripling renewable energy production by 2030, as agreed during COP28 in Dubai, is the most effective way to reduce emissions. Once dependent on oil shale, Estonia now generates around 40% of its electricity from renewables, with solar capacity growing 25 times in just five years. By 2035, we aim for 80% clean electricity. Together with Finland and Latvia, we are building new electricity connections to support renewable energy. We will soon adopt the Climate Resilience Economy Act, aligning climate, economic, and nature policies. By law, 30% of land and sea will be protected, and the new vehicle tax is already steering drivers towards cleaner cars. Colleagues, innovation is central to our approach. Estonia developed smart rainwater system to reduce flood risks and applies digital and responsible AI tools for smart energy, precision agriculture, and climate monitoring. These strengthen resilience and evidence-based policymaking. As new technologies can also sometimes bring along environmental impacts and dependencies, the green transition must remain sustainable. Estonia shares our technical and digital expertise globally and contributes 1.5 million euro annually to developing countries to tackle climate change. Yet, nearly 20% of the world still lacks electricity and over 2 billion people rely on polluting cooking fuels that harm both health and the environment, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa. With solar and wind now affordable, clean energy must reach everyone. Finally, Russia's war against Ukraine reminds us that conflict intensifies environmental destruction and global insecurity, with constant bombardments poisoning ecosystems and harming health. This is not a moment for despair, but it is for determination and deliberate action. It is a moment to take stock, recalibrate, and prepare for the hard work that needs to be done at COP30 in Brazil. And in Belem, countries will need to respond with a clear plan to close the ambition gap, along with the gaps in ambition on adaptation and finance. It's therefore essential that COP30, under the leadership of Brazil, delivers a bold and credible response to the NDC ambition gap and signals that 2025 represents a turning point. the beginning of a decade of acceleration, delivery, and implementation.
